text: OH hello there. I actually did see you,  because I am an all seeing being. And if you’re
hallucinating me right now, that just means that  you’re on your first steps in the hero’s journey.
You’re going to achieve the  impossible, rise against
all odds, make fame and fortune for  generations of offspring to come.
Unless your name is BRIAN. All Brians suck, I am  so sorry that’s just in your DNA. There’s never
been a hero named Brian, and if there was  I assure you, that was not their real name.
I’m sorry, Brian watching this, but you should  have known better. You should’ve been born
someone else. Anyways. Did you guys know  that clouds are made out of marshmallows?
You’d think cotton candy, but no, the store  was out of cotton candy so, marshmallows.
Anyways. Everyone else, you can  go off, hero-ing! Except you
BRIAN you’re gonna sit there and  think about what you might have done.
Most of us know what the hero’s  journey, or the “monomyth”
is even if you think you don’t. It’s the idea  that all the myths in human history can be
simplified down into one common form. The  concept was invented and popularized by
writer and professor Joseph Campbell in his  book HERO WITH A THOUSAND FACES from 1949.
You’ve probably seen this handy little diagram  in an English class or a screenwriting class.
The hero starts at home; crosses the  threshold into a larger, strange world;
faces trials, and is transformed; eventually  returning home, a changed person. For example,
Star Wars, one of the most  influential films of all time,
was literally written by George Lucas  with the hero’s journey in mind.
[Star Wars theme] I didn’t have a harp.
It’s become the gold standard for how to tell  the story of a hero. Campbell read thousands of
myths from all over the world, all different  time periods, and argued that all of them,
that’s right all of them, can be boiled down into  this series of steps. “Well that seems a little
reductive,” you might think. And to that I would  say, who are you talking to, me explaining Joseph
Campbell’s theory? Or Joseph Campbell’s theory?  Because the answer to your question is: YES.
In his book on the Monomyth,  Campbell describes the hero as:
“the man or woman who has been able to battle  past his personal and local historical limitations
to the generally valid, normally human forms.  [His] visions, ideas, and inspirations come
pristine from the primary springs of human life  and thought. [Hence] They are eloquent, not of
the present, disintegrating society and psyche,  but of the unquenched source through which society
is reborn.” He is an “eternal man–perfected,  unspecific, universal man–he has been reborn.”
Campbell argues that we can take  a specific person, whether it’s an
ancient myth or a modern hero, pull them  out of their time and place, and voila:
they are all the same. And on the one hand, you  could see this as a way that we are all united
in our humanity, that no matter the culture  or time there are certain truths we uphold.
BUT the “universal truths” that Campbell suggests,  just happen to be dripping in his own biases,
fantasies, upbringing, culture, and the  now extremely outdated white hetero male
Christian worldview of someone raised in early  20th century America. In other words, whoof.
In his writing about the history  of humanity reciting stories,
Campbell uses words like “normal” and “generally  valid” as if those are completely agreed upon
values throughout all of time (they’re not.)  He acts as though he is above the influence of
time and place and that his opinions  are objectively universal and essential
(they’re not.) He claims that a hero is  “perfected, unspecific, universal,” as
if heroes have been made on an assembly line  for thousands of years, instead of each saying
something about the time and place they originate  from (a third parenthetical). And you know what,
sure, instead of doing the work to understand a  different culture’s perspective it WOULD be easier
if they all just happen to fit into the template  you made up. So you know what, you got me there.
Campbell often assures us that every myth has  one, objective reading and point of view. But
even with a passing knowledge of Western mythology  you know that that is ABSOLUTELY not true!!!
Odysseus, one of the most famous mythic heroes,  was a clever hero to the Greeks. But to the Romans
he was a deceitful villain, even calling him  “cruel Odysseus.” The Greek playwright Sophocles
portrayed Odysseus in completely different ways  even within his own plays: a “commonsensical
realist” in Ajax, but a “scheming sophist” in  Philoctetes. So. Which one is the objective
truth of the myth of Odysseus? Ironically, one  of the actual consistent themes of The Odyssey
is that there IS no objective retelling  of events. It is the storyteller who is
motivated to tell the tale in a specific way,  for a specific reason, to a specific audience,
with a specific goal in mind. And although Joseph  Campbell likes to see himself as the ultimate
objective voice speaking for all of humanity, at  the end of the day he too is simply a storyteller,
motivated to tell his tale in a specific way, for  a specific reason, with a specific goal in mind,
with all of his biases and motives in tact.  The way he strips myths of culture and intent
mirrors the way he wishes to strip himself of  culture and intent. A perfect man, unbeholden to
the timeline of history. A hero, he might say,  about himself. But here’s the objective truth:
Campbell is very much beholden to his time and  place, as are the stories we tell. And the journey
of understanding someone else’s perspective  is much more worthwhile, one that has the real
danger of challenging our own point of view and  assumptions about the world, but has the potential
to shape us into a better person than who we  were before we stepped outside our front door.
It probably helps to understand Joseph Campbell  if I tell you that he was a raging misogynist
who believed women could NOT be heroes they  are just prizes at the end FOR the hero
and the closest they can get is by giving birth,  and also he taught at an all women’s college,
telling them all that they can’t be heroes, and  when I tell you his ideas have shaped the way
we live and especially shaped the worldview of  men who ARE told to see themselves as the hero
of their own mythic tale, I MEAN IT. But  hey, don’t take my word for it, take his:
“All [women] have to do is stop looking at the  boys and wondering whether they are in competition
with them. Just realize what effect they are  having on the boys. It came to me at Sarah
Lawrence [at the time, an all female college].  I was teaching these courses on mythology and at
the end of my last year there this woman comes  in and sits down and says, ‘Well, Mr Campbell,
you’ve been talking about the hero. But what  about the woman?’ / I said, ‘The woman’s the
mother of the hero; she’s the goal of the hero’s  achieving; she’s the protectress of the hero;
she is this, she is that. What more do  you want?’ / She said, ‘I want to be the
hero!’ / So I was glad that I was retiring that  year and not going to teach any more [laughter].”
[chewing]
In Stories About Stories, writer and  professor Brian Attebery points out
the limits of Campbell’s mythic system: “In  The Hero With 1000 Faces, Campbell makes much
of the Navajo story about the Twin War Gods  who go on a quest for their father the Sun.
They fit his pattern. He says  nothing about Coyote, who doesn’t.
Other Navajo figures get turned into accessories  to the hero’s tale. Spider Woman, for instance,
the great weaver who created everything, is  dismissed as a ‘grandmotherly little dame
who lives underground’ and whose function  is primarily to help the Twin Heroes.”
I cannot stress how much this little graph has  shaped the world around us. It’s used in Hollywood
TODAY as the only, objective, template  for every story. Pretty much every book
on screenwriting recycles a version of his  hero’s journey template. And why wouldn’t they?
Campbell asserts with every other breath that  he’s “figured it out!” He’s given you The Key
to storytelling! To deviate from it would be as  perverse as raging against the machine! Which
maybe explains why sometimes stories  from Hollywood feel so… same-y.
Executives, producers, all the way down to your  professors and fellow creators are giving feedback
and notes based off of this guy’s ideas from the  1950s, and I don’t know if you know the 1950s,
but it doesn’t take long to figure out that maybe  he might have missed the mark on a thing or two.
And his influence doesn’t stop at Hollywood  storytelling, Campbell’s ideas affect our everyday
lives, what we’re allowed to become, how we see  ourselves, how others treat us. You can see his
influence on everything from the current stripping  of women and pregnant people’s bodily autonomy,
to the fantasy narrative that a “good guy  with a gun” is gonna show up and save us all.
In a very real, and tangible way, he has limited  our imagination of who and what makes a hero.
To know the man’s work, we should first take a  look at the man, Joseph Campbell himself. What
did he believe? Why did he believe it? This  is an easier question to ask than to answer,
because Campbell himself was EXTREMELY  inconsistent in his own views.
Campbell grew up idolizing Douglas Fairbanks,  the silent movie star from films like Robin
Hood and Zorro. This is probably why Campbell  considers himself a “maverick.” “I see myself
as a maverick.” If there was a machine? Campbell  would totally rage against it. He’s against rigid
structural systems, just like the hero outsiders  of his childhood soaps. “How in heaven’s name are
you going to find your own track if you are always  doing what society tells you to do? I [also]
spent a year teaching in a boy’s prep school…  those who followed their zeal, their bliss,
they have led decent, wonderful lives; those who  did what Dad said they should do because it’s safe
found out it’s not safe. It’s disaster.” But this  quote is in the middle of a 300 page book about
his extremely rigid Hero’s Cycle structure, one so  innate to human nature that supposedly no one has
ever crafted tales that deviate from it (we have.)  He often repeats societal norms from his time as
immutable truths, things that are now completely  outdated: everything from gender roles, to gender
expression, to compulsatory heterosexuality,  even Protestant work ethic are all set in stone.
He insists that he and the heroes he  recognizes should rebel against these systems,
while also reassuring himself and the heroes that  he recognizes, that the world is actually perfect
and doesn’t need to change. Here’s Campbell saying  as much from The Power of Myth, the PBS series
that did a lot to secure his place in pop culture  infamy: “When people say to me you know ‘Do you
have optimism about the world you know, how  terrible it is?’ I said, ‘Yes, it’s great… just
the way it is!” That people like him should work  within the systems: “I don’t think it would help
you to change the system, but it would help you  to live in the system as a human being.” This is
like saying at the end of Star Wars, Luke should  have joined the empire. Which, bold move, Cotton.
His mantra, which you’ve probably heard not  knowing it came from him, I certainly didn’t,
is “Follow your bliss.” “If you do follow  your bliss, you put yourself on a kind of
track that has been there all the while, waiting  for you, and the life that you ought to be living
is the one you are living, somehow… If you are  following your bliss, you are having that joy,
that refreshment, that life all the time.” Which  does sound nice. It sounds like he is saying
know yourself intimately, follow your heart,  lead with bravery and good things will happen.
“Follow your bliss, I mean find where it is, and  don’t be afraid to follow it.” “If the work that
you’re doing is the work that you chose to do  because you’re enjoying it, then that’s it.
But if you think oh gee I couldn’t do that,  you know, that’s your dragon locking you in.”
Looking around at the “current state of things,”
seeing all the unionizing and workers coming  together having to fight for basic human decency,
it’s clear his point of view comes  from a place of extreme privilege.
Oh, you didn’t quit your job to live in your  van? You must not be brave enough! Nevermind that
you have a kid and you need to keep your health  insurance. His framework of bravery is exclusively
for those who have the social mobility and hard  power – cough cough white men – to make selfish
choices. He never examines anything further than  this, he doesn’t entertain the nuance that your
“follow your bliss” could be someone else’s “my  mom couldn’t stock the refrigerator this month.”
Campbell is arguing that if you’re  stuck in the dead end job that you hate,
it’s entirely your own fault. You’re just  not being heroic enough. You’re failing on an
existential level to live your life the right  way. It’s an individual problem, rather than
a structural problem. And the only way to escape  is to follow his series of steps. Which is pretty
convenient for him because he doesn’t believe we  need to fundamentally change anything anyways.
Don’t get me wrong, Campbell HAS faced hardships.  Like when he was unemployed for five years during
the Great Depression and he… wait, am I reading  this correctly? He didn’t need a job except “dog
sitting” for a friend? And he had the free time  to read for 9 HOURS A DAY. For five years! Oh my
gosh that’s so cool, before I did YouTube I WISH  I also dog-sat, as one of the SEVEN jobs that I
had so I could just pay my rent. His description  of this time sounds exactly like a celebrity
recounting their “daily routine.” His advice  to other people is that he created a schedule,
which like, GOOD FOR YOU I GUESS YOU DIDN’T HAVE  ADHD. Let alone another human to take care of,
or a police state monitoring your every waking  breath, or seemingly responsibilities other
than going to the occasional cocktail party.  Which he did include time for in his schedule.
Brendan Gill, a journalist and associate  of Campbell, criticized him in 1989,
saying: “Far from being spiritual,  it is intensely materialistic;
my old spellbinding friend is preaching  a doctrine similar to that which Ayn Rand
voiced in her novel, The Fountainhead.” Gill went  on to compare Campbell’s “do whatever makes you
happy” idea to the selfishness and greed of  Reagan, Thatcher, and Wall Street yuppies.
“The most conspicuous members of our society.”  “Greed, for lack of a better word, is good.”
Already, we’re not starting off on a great journey  together. But it’s not only the big ideas that
Campbell contradicts himself on constantly.  It’s even small details like, are computers
good or bad? He recounts this tale of President  Eisenhower going into a room full of computers,
“He puts the question to these machines, ‘Is there  a God?’ and there’s all those lights flashing and
wheels turning and things like that. And  after about 10 minutes of that kind of thing,
a voice comes forth and the  voice says, ‘Now there is.’” Ohh,
spooky. But moments later talking  about how all those little microchips?
They’re tiny little angels. “Have you ever looked  inside one of those things? You can’t believe it.
It’s a whole hierarchy of angels all on slats.  Those are miracles, they’re miracles. They are.”
So, are computers good or bad? If they’re  challenging my worldview of a God in heaven,
they’re bad. “I am God here!” But if they’re doing  what I want, they’re angels. “Are you an angel?”
Is the machine of society bad? Or is  it proof of man’s greatness? While he
criticizes “The machine,” and speaks of  the “individual” fighting against “the
state,” “And this is the threat to our lives,  we all face it. We all operate in our society
in relation to a system.” He also romanticizes  the massive New York skyscrapers that epitomize
the cold, inhuman machine of American  capitalism: “You can tell what’s informing
society by the size of–what the building is that’s  the tallest building in the place… The temple was
built right in the center of the city. This is the  proper organization, that’s the spiritual center
from which all flows in all directions. And then  the capitol was built right beside the temple...
And now the biggest thing is the office building  that takes care of the affairs of both the temple
and the political building. That’s the history  of Western civilization.” I really cut this down
because he keeps jazzing about skyscrapers,  he continues: “In New York now the debate
is over who can build the tallest building not  to praise, but to build the tallest building.”
“And they are magnificent. We are a financial  power center, and look what we can do. It’s a
kind of virtuosic acrobatic stunt.” Ah yes, I am  so inspired when the beautiful Chicago skyline
is interrupted by a phallic TRUMP TOWER  blocking the view of Lake Michigan.
Brendan Gill directly compared Joseph  Campbell with the character Roark from
Ayn Rand’s The Fountainhead: “The creator lives  for his work,” says Roark. “He needs no other men.
His primary goal is within himself…. The man  who attempts to live for others is…a parasite
in motive and makes parasites of those he serves.”  Two years before The Fountainhead was published,
young Campbell was saying at Sarah Lawrence,  “The artist—insofar as he is an artist—looks
at the world dispassionately: without  thought of defending his ego or his friends,
without thought of undoing an enemy; troubled  neither with desire nor with loathing.”
Ah yes, Ayn Rand, the ultimate pick me girl.
The final boss of girlbosses. “Before you can  do things for people, you must be the kind of
man who can get things done. But! To get things  done, you must love the doing, not the people.”
In everything that Campbell does, he claims that  a small, certain archetype – that of the brooding,
unfeeling, stoic man – is the everyman.
Everywhere he looks he sees himself, and  where he doesn’t, he doesn’t see a hero.
Here’s Brian Attebery again: “The problem  with Campbell’s monomyth as an analytical tool
is that it always works because it simplifies  every story to the point where nothing but the
monomyth is left. It ignores the many mythic  stories that do not have questing heroes,
and it leaves out the culturally defined values  and symbols that make each tradition unique.”
Well, let’s see, we covered machines,  skyscrapers, computers, what was that
other thing that he was obsessed with? Oh, that’s  right. Everyone is being too hard on the Nazis.
Yeah, you heard that right. Okay!  I’m gonna need an intermission.
To throw up all of those marshmallows that I ate.
